speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DISARMAMENT
subsubtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO ORGANIZE COMMON POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that the flurry from the opposition benches is over I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister with all due and proper respect for parliamentary procedure.
In view of the most significant peacetime announcement by Right Hon. Harold Macmillan, Prime Minister of Great Britain, that he intends to attempt to organize a commonwealth policy on disarmament at the commonwealth conference of prime ministers to be held in London next month, can the Prime Minister inform the house whether the government has given consideration to this announcement and its response to the same?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
subsubtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO ORGANIZE COMMON POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have received no indication that the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, to use the words of the hon. gentleman, "intends to organize a commonwealth policy on disarmament". Such a course, I think, would be foreign to the relationship among the countries of the commonwealth. However, it is the practice of these conferences to endeavour to arrive at a consensus of opinion on various issues that are of importance to the various nations comprising the commonwealth family.
One of these issues is the question of disarmament, which I know will receive full attention from those in attendance at that conference. As I said the other day-I believe on February 3-in answer to the hon. member for Essex East, in our discussions I do not think it would be appropriate to attempt to arrive at a common policy applicable to


all parts of the commonwealth. We will discuss, consider, and I am sure agree on the need of furthering every effort toward disarmament. That has been the purpose of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom throughout the last several years, particularly evidenced by the fact that he has sought the closest relationships between east and west consistent with the maintenance and preservation of freedom. That has been the attitude of this government, as I stated the other day, and that is the attitude of the other governments of the commonwealth. My hope is that in the discussions to be held all of us will be able to attain a unity in our objectives without in any way interfering with the basic principles of the commonwealth.

The announcement was made in Washington by the President at his press conference this morning. It would have been made in the House of Commons at the same time if it had been possible to do so. The reason it was not made in the house was that it was agreed that the announcement would be made on Wednesday, and I think it is only fair to advise the house accordingly.
Incidentally, the President said this morning that it was a good thing internationally for old friends to get together. I am looking forward to this meeting, which will be an informal one, free from any formal connotations. I think it is desirable that, as one of the representatives of Canada at the prime ministers' conference, I should be enabled to have at first hand the views of our close and highly regarded neighbour on the many questions which will be coming before the conference.

Mr. Speaker, this subject has been discussed between both governments, and I think a full report has been given on the question. If the facts are as stated by the Leader of the Opposition, naturally it is a matter that should continue to be discussed between our countries. However, within the time limit available to me on this occasion I am not certain that this will be one of the subjects discussed.

As he knows, agreements were entered into some five or six years ago. The result of these open end agreements, of course, has been that the Canadian uranium industry has found itself in a difficult position. I am sure I do not need to tell the hon. gentleman this, but continuing representations are made on this subject.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED IMPORTS OF VEGETABLES FROM CUBA
speechtext:
Yesterday a question was asked by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska with respect to imports of tomatoes from Cuba. My department is aware of the current movement of Cuban tomatoes into Canada. However, the movement from Florida is by rail rather than by truck. These tomatoes do not compete with the production of Ontario growers, since there are no Canadian tomatoes on the market at present and marketing in commercial volume is not expected prior to the latter part of March.
Starting April 1, all imported tomatoes will be subject to a duty of 10 per cent ad valorem. This will continue until the seasonal specific duty of 1% cents per pound is applied for a period of 32 weeks, usually starting in the latter part of June in Ontario.
In regard to the supplementary question, I would inform the house that these shipments have conformed to the provisions of section 56 of the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 7, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Churchill-Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Pension Act to provide for increases to disabled veterans and their dependents; to permit payment of supplementary pensions in certain cases; to permit appeals from decisions of the former board of pension commissioners; and to provide for certain further changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Pension Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, prior to the adjournment of the house last night I had been referring to pension advocates. I may say I brought this matter up as a member of the standing committee on veterans affairs. My opinion is that throughout all the years these pension advocates have never been brought together for a refresher course.
I submit the minister should look into this aspect of the matter. If the pension advocates were brought in for a refresher course, they could brush up on pension law, and I believe that it would help a great deal in the work. This would be following a practice that most organizations find helpful. I think this is most important, because it means a lot to the veteran in the preparation and presentation of his claim. In general, the pension advocates are doing a good job, but if they were brought together and given the opportunity to exchange ideas they would go back to work with new confidence and new ideas and do a better job.
My final observation is in connection with the proposed legislation. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that at the outset I said that the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act were complementary one to the other. I would hope that certain amendments would be made to the War Veterans Allowance Act in order to conform with the increase in disability pensions. I have in mind a recipient who, for instance, is receiving a 10 per cent disability pension and at the same time is receiving war veterans allowance. Under the proposed amendment this recipient will receive an increase in the disability pension and under present regulations he will have his war veterans allowance decreased, a procedure which will in effect nullify the proposed increase. I hope provision will be made so that the recipients referred to will enjoy the proposed increases.
I do not suppose any provision is made in the proposed legislation or in the bill to come before the house, but I should hope that this matter will receive attention shortly so the recipients may enjoy the increase. If we do not do this, I think a great deal of confusion is going to be caused, and certainly a great deal of disappointment.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee on veterans affairs I wish to say a word of commendation on the introduction of amendments to the act which will provide for pension increases to disabled veterans and their dependents. I also wish to join with those who preceded me in this debate in extending to the minister congratulations on his appointment to one of the less controversial departments of the government. When I say this, I do not mean to convey the impression that there is always

Pension Act
agreement. However, on the whole the humanitarian aspect of the Department of Veterans Affairs is such that it does not offer the same area of conflict in ideas, because the subject is protected by a universal appeal to the better instincts of the members.
During the last two sessions of parliament I had the privilege of serving on the committee on veterans affairs, and at the numerous committee meetings which were held during those two sessions delegations were heard and many recommendations relating to the Pension Act were placed before the committee. This was, of course, to be expected. ft is only natural that the most important subject of discussion at these committee meetings had to do with compensation for disabilities suffered by men in the service of the country. Throughout the course of the deliberations the then minister-he is now a member of the other place-who was indeed friendly, patient and even sympathetic to the problems of veterans, made it clear then that the Pension Act would not be up for amendment, but he intimated that in 1961 the act would come under review. I am therefore pleased that at last the amendments are being made in a revision which I hope will result in a fair increase in the pensions of veterans in order to enable them to meet the present-day cost of living.
As a matter of justice these pensions should be under constant review, and should not be allowed to be dormant or fixed for years. The Canadian Legion and the war veterans associations have recommended an increase in pensions across the board. We on this side of the house feel that this recommendation should be considered along with the pension for the disabled veterans.
Then there is the question of the Hong Kong veterans. A delegation of this organization appeared before the committee and renewed their appeal for special compensation. It is a problem which should be well known to the government and which also merits special consideration.
One of the matters that illustrates the crying need for revision of the act is certainly the ceiling on a veterans income, which is $145 a month for a married man. I have in my constituency several cases in which veterans are being penalized because they have been able to supplement their meagre allowance with odd jobs, and in some instances because their wives are working part time, something they do only because it is their only means of meeting expenses and providing not luxuries but bare necessities. Thank you, Mr. Chairman; I shall omit reading the communication which I intended to read. However, I should like to point out one single phase which I think is pertinent to the discussion of this subject. This particular veteran at one point, in view of his eyesight not being good, applied to the Department of Veterans Affairs at Winnipeg. This man lives in Fort William. He wanted to get a pair of glasses which cost $28 in Fort William. He received from the veterans welfare officer a communication which in effect said this:
Our Winnipeg office advises me that you wrote to the director general, treatment services, regarding glasses. I understand that you have been advised that these cannot be provided unless you are prepared to go to Winnipeg at your own expense.

It would cost at least $100 for a man to travel from Fort William to Winnipeg, wait probably two or three days to obtain a pair of free glasses, and return to Fort William. He could buy these glasses in Fort William for only about $28. I am merely pointing out the seeming lack of liaison among the various offices of the D.V.A.
Of course no Canadian war veteran should have to apply for charity for himself or his family, and I express the hope that the resolution we are debating today and which has been debated during the past few days will precede the enactment of legislation which will make unnecessary the humiliating recourse to public welfare. I think this is important.
The recommendations placed before the committee during both the 1959 and 1960 sessions of parliament by several veterans organizations have been most helpful to the members of the committee. I can also say that these submissions were made with dignity and restraint. There was, for example, the resolution submitted by the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans in Canada which had been approved at their 1960 dominion convention. I wish to quote the resolution; surely this would not be out of order:
Whereas the Pension Act states that in any application for pension, the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt and the adjudicating body is directed to draw all reasonably inference in favour of the applicant; and
Whereas the pension commission, the pension appeal board and medical authorities acting on their behalf, are not in many cases giving the veteran the benefit of the doubt;
Therefore be it resolved by the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans in Canada, in dominion convention assembled, that this obvious violation of the Pension Act be again called to the attention of the various bodies who adjudicate upon pension applications and be duly reminded of their statutory duty to give to the applicant the benefit of the doubt according to the clear and specific terms of the section above mentioned;
I commend to the minister the suggestions contained in this resolution and express the hope that they will receive favourable consideration. They are suggestions which should be considered by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
During the course of the debate on this bill we will have another opportunity to review the exact amendments which are proposed by the government. At the present time we can only speak in generalities, and that is one of the reasons I have pointed out the complaints and suggestions which I have received from many of my constituents. We hope that the considerations mentioned in this house during the passage of the bill will meet with the approval and approbation of our veterans, especially those who are in need of assistance.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising this afternoon to say a few brief words on this resolution I should first like to join previous speakers in expressing my compliments to the new Minister of Veterans Affairs. He is a man who has rendered great service to his country in two wars. He is well known for his interest in veterans affairs throughout his public life and even in his private life. Since taking over this important portfolio he has demonstrated that he has the interest of veterans at heart, and I am sure they can expect him to give very great consideration to the many problems which still face those who served our country in time of war.
I should also like to pay tribute to my old friend the immediate past minister in this portfolio, Hon. Alfred J. Brooks. He also gave great service to his country and throughout his public lifetime displayed a very personal interest in the problems of those comrades with whom he served and who fought for their country in the first and second world wars.
It is hard for me, as a pensioner myself, to define the term "disability pension". I would rather refer to it as an earnest desire by a grateful people to compensate others for a part of their physical being given up in service to the country.
The proposed increase which is before the house will be welcomed not only by pensioners but by their comrades the other veterans, and by all people in this country who take some pride in the fact that we still live in a free country. Not all pensioners will definitely need this increased financial assistance, in the sense of a necessity to put daily bread on the table. But I would point out that everyone in this country has a responsibility, including those who suffer from disability.
The pensioner, like anyone else, has obligations to his family, to his friends and to the community at large. A disabled person does not have the same chance to fulfil these obligations; therefore he or she must do other things to compensate for that deficiency. With an increase in remuneration, this money can go some way toward filling this gap. Not only will this proposal today benefit the pensioner himself, but it will bring great benefit to those around him and to the community at large.
There is one aspect of the resolution as explained by the minister which is very commendable. This legislation seeks to plug some gaps in the set-up. No matter how well things are set up to provide for the many, there are always the few who seem to be on the fringe and who are called upon to suffer under certain circumstances. I am very pleased to see that this resolution at

Pension Act
least tends to plug some of those gaps. I would recommend that the minister and all those who are concerned with this or other veterans' legislation look into the many other gaps which still exist.
On other occasions in this house I have expressed my concern regarding the older veterans, the veterans of wars prior to 1939. These men have now reached the eve of their lives. Many of them do not have too many years to look forward to. Many are drawing small disability pensions supplemented by war veterans allowances. The implementation of this increased pension will not bring any fuller benefit to many of these people. I would therefore urge the minister to give every consideration to an early review of the War Veterans Allowance Act in order that some additional benefit may accrue to these people who because of age and infirmity are deserving of some comfort in their few remaining years.
I do not intend to take any more of the time of the committee at this stage. I am anxious as I am sure are all hon. members and the people of Canada to see what is contained in this bill. I will now resume my place and if there is anything further I have to say I shall bring it up when the bill is before us.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is legislation to increase pensions for disabled veterans and their dependents. The resolution further aims at adding new provisions and introducing certain amendments to the act.
At this time, we are being asked to approve the principle of those increases, without knowing their scope. When we have the bill before us, we will be in a better position to appreciate its scope and, if necessary, to criticize the bill if we find it inadequate to meet the veterans' present needs.
There is no doubt that, in principle, the resolution is welcomed by all hon. members in this house. We all have, in our respective constituencies, veterans of the two world wars, and of the Korean war. We are so much indebted to them that we should never miss an opportunity to provide the greatest possible security for them and their dependents.
In this respect, I would like to take the opportunity of this resolution to say a word or two on the present position of our veterans, a great number of whom-and I know 
the present minister is quite familiar with the situation-have had great difficulty in readjusting to civilian life and are in a sad plight because of present economic conditions and prevailing unemployment.
In that light, I think the government is not giving the veterans the help and support required to meet their needs and those of their families.
I followed yesterday with great interest and some curiosity the highly emotional speech made by the Associate Minister of National Defence. It was a fine piece of oratory, but I am trying in vain to find anything which might be of practical assistance to our veterans in dealing with their problems. It is certainly not with such speeches that their position will be improved.
The Associate Minister of National Defence was very cautious. He referred only briefly to the economic angle, as can be seen on page 1809 of Hansard, where he is quoted as saying:
This increase will stave off the destitution which unfortunately threatens quite a few of our veterans.
We would have liked the Associate Minister of National Defence to elaborate on that point, because he himself is a veteran with a very distinguished record in the last war, of which he can rightly be proud. But that is not the point. Our responsibility as legislators is rather a question of enacting practical legislation to help a class of people-in this case the veterans-who are given a privileged position, and rightly so, with regard to employment in the civil service. However, when it comes to awarding jobs, it does not seem that we are doing enough at this time to help a class of citizens to whom we are so greatly indebted.
The Associate Minister of National Defence, as well as other members on the government side, rather skipped over the political aspect in yesterday's speeches. Indeed, on the basis of their statements, one might think the world only started in 1957. Now, with all due respect to the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill) and to the former minister (Mr. Brooks), there have also been other ministers of veterans affairs in the past few years. There was the Hon. Milton Gregg who, if I remember correctly, was not only a veteran, but a recipient of the Victoria Cross. There was the Hon. Ian Mackenzie and the Hon. Hugues Lapointe.

They were all veterans, and today, it is simply a matter of amending a piece of Liberal legislation. Indeed, we took such good care of our veterans in the years preceding 1957, that the Associate Minister of National Defence, in his address, unconsciously recognized it when he said, and I quote from page 1809 of Hansard:
When I came back from the war in 1945, I was fairly discouraged, and if it had not been for the good care and encouragement I received in veterans hospitals, I wonder whether my convalescence would have been as short, and if I could have made such rapid progress as I did.
He was thus paying tribute to former Liberal ministers of veterans affairs, and I am delighted to have this opportunity today to put the record straight.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in our constituencies we are very often visited by veterans. They are usually in trying and distressing circumstances, and we refer them to the veterans' office on McGill street in Montreal. Now, everyone knows that the staff of that office cannot do a thing to help them at the present time, for all their good intentions. So without minimizing the good effects of this legislation, I would have liked the many Conservative members who took the floor to laud the government for introducing this legislation, to soft-pedal their praise and recognize the hard fact that the first thing our veterans want is jobs. That is what they want. And they are the first to suffer from the situation in which the government has placed them for the last two or three years. That is what I should like the government, and particularly the Minister of Veterans Affairs, to keep in mind in introducing the bill which will follow this resolution.
Under present conditions, veterans' preference, as applied under the provisions of the existing legislation, does not mean a thing, because there are no jobs. Again, without minimizing the possible importance of this bill I say it does not go far enough, and that very special consideration should be given our veterans who are the first to suffer from the unemployment problem facing us today.
I hope that before introducing his bill, the Minister of Veterans Affairs will take these remarks into consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, from the year 1920 until 1957 veterans pensions have been increased on but three different occasions. Let me quote single rates. The first increase came
90205-6-118
Pension Act
in 1947 when the amount for a single 100 per cent disability pensioner was increased from $900 yearly to $1,128. Then in 1951 this amount was raised to $1,500 yearly, and finally, in 1957, it was raised from $1,500 to $1,800. Thus we see that over a period of some 37 years only three increases have been granted, or an average of one increase for approximately every 12 years.
If we take the increase of 1957 and the one proposed in the resolution before us we note that we shall have had two increases in a little over three years, or an average of approximately one increase for every one and a half years since 1957. I give these averages merely to indicate that the interest of the government on behalf of our veterans is steadily and rapidly increasing rather than diminishing as the years pass.
As further testimony of this fact we need only to mention the emergence of the veterans charter following world war II, the setting up of the standing committee on veterans affairs in 1958, and the work undertaken by that committee since its inception. Its review of some four pieces of legislation and subsequent amendment and improvement by this house all bear witness to the ever growing interest in the affairs of our Canadian veterans.
The present resolution before us and what it will mean for our disabled veterans are very warmly welcomed on all sides of this house and across the country generally. Like others who have spoken on this resolution, I warmly congratulate and commend the minister on having introduced it. Since I am mindful of the keen and broad interest which such a subject arouses and realize that every constituency in Canada will experience the favourable results, my words will be brief in order to assure time for many others who I know would like to make their comments.
Of the approximately 20 members who have already spoken on this resolution I have noted that the majority expressed some dissatisfaction with the pensions commission application of section 70, or the benefit of the doubt clause. I, too, very strongly feel that the commission is not carrying out the intent of parliament in many of its decisions which adversely affect our veterans. The purpose or intent of section 70, as set out by parliament, permits, if not instructs, that body to give the veteran the benefit of the doubt when further or more conclusive medical evidence is desirable before award. In many instances, as has already been pointed out, it would appear that instead of such interpretation the board has taken the view that sufficient and conclusive evidence

Pension Act
should be presented to the degree that there can be no element of doubt in their minds that an award is justified. I sincerely hope that in the future the original and actual intent of parliament will be more carefully observed and that as a result a greater and a completely justified leniency will be shown the claimants.
I realize that at times the veteran, or the person or persons preparing and compiling his evidence, may be partially at fault in not doing a more thorough job. This necessitates appeals and abhorrent delays. Here I wish to pay a special word of tribute to the service officers at dominion command here in Ottawa for their efficient and excellent work on behalf of veterans of this country, and more particularly on behalf of veterans in my constituency, of which I have a firsthand knowledge. Identical words of praise go also to our district pensions advocate in the Halifax office.
I should like to devote some time to what I feel would be a consideration of desirable and timely changes in our war veterans allowances legislation. However, since it is the Pension Act which is before us, and with the hope that an opportunity will be provided us in the veterans affairs committee to consider this matter which is so closely and directly allied with pensions themselves, I will desist at this time.
In conclusion, I merely wish to say that as a veteran, as a member of the standing committee on veterans affairs and as a backbencher from a very important constituency I wish to thank the government and the minister sincerely for having introduced this resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to join with previous speakers in expressing my best wishes to our new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill). Because of his military reputation and because he took part in the last two wars, we are sure that the minister will give consideration to our veterans' problems and solve them by meeting their requests, which are justified since these people sacrificed their lives to protect the freedoms we hold dear.
At the same time, I want to thank the former minister of veterans affairs, Colonel Brooks, who, with the government, amended the legislation to give the veterans part of their due.
I heard the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) say earlier that before we came to office, veterans had been well taken care of. Let me tell the hon. member that as soon as the Conservative party came into power, one of the first acts to be adopted was that which increased veterans allowances by 17 per cent, while during their three last years in power, our friends had granted them only an increase of a mere 3 per cent.
I will go further and say that during 1956 and 1957 their government spent only $130 million on that score, while in 1959 and 1960 our veterans and their dependents have received an increase of $149 million. We of the Conservative party are devoted to the cause of our veterans; I would even say that we are the first government of Canada to have in our ranks so many veterans.
The Hon. Mr. Brooks and his government have amended the act to allow the benefits to be paid from the special fund provided by the War Veterans Allowance Act, which means an increase of 410 per cent under our administration.
So, may I point out again to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont that we did more during the three years we have been in office than the government of which he was a member did during the period from 1945 to 1956. Besides, by this resolution, we intend to increase further the allowances and benefits paid to those who fought for us during the last two wars. In fact, I notice that we want to authorize the payment of additional pensions in certain cases and permit appeals from decisions of the former pension board.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out to the minister that on several occasions veterans have come to me with their case. I am really surprised that the Canadian pension commission should refuse either an increase or a pension to certain veterans. The decision is always based on the famous section-I think it is section 7-concerning marginal cases. I think that a man who served in the Canadian army either during the 1914-18 war or during the 1939-45 war, who underwent intense training, who fought in France and Italy, certainly lost part of his health there even if he was not wounded. Therefore I repeat that I am surprised that the commission should never give those veterans the benefit of the doubt.
I should like to draw the minister's attention to one particular case. A certain Mr. Bergeron, a resident of my constituency,

served six years in the army, that is, from 1939 to 1945; he served in France and in Germany, and during his period of service he was treated for rheumatism and was confined for 15 days. Now, the Canadian pension commission refuses to recognize that this man had to leave his job because he could not continue to fulfil his duties on account of his health, and the commission will not award him a certain percentage of pension although he contracted that disease while serving in the army.
I have another case, that of a certain Mr. Grandisson concerning whom a letter dated February 3 was addressed to me. This man receives a 40 per cent disability pension. He lost a lung as a result of a wound suffered in action and his doctors will not let him work because he cannot even handle a shovel. The pension commission refuses to award him an increase or find him a job at the veterans hospital.
I should like through you, Mr. Chairman, to draw the minister's attention to those two cases I have just mentioned, so that the Canadian pension commission would forget sometimes that the veteran making an application has no intention of obtaining money to which he is not entitled, but merely what is due to him for his sacrifices during the war as a compensation for losing his health while serving his country.
There is another point that I should like to raise. There are in our ranks and outside our party today people who fought in the last two world wars, the first from 1914 to 1918, and the second from 1939 to 1945. On their discharge, they were enjoying perfect health, but today, at the age of 55, 60 or 65, they are afflicted with certain illnesses. I am not asking for a pension on their behalf, because they do not want any. But those veterans should at least get free hospital care.
I am sure that after five or ten years of war service, the incapacities afflicting those veterans today are due in great part to their military service.
Speaking of hospitals, I should like to point out to you that several veterans who are friends of mine come and tell me that there is certainly room for improvement in the Ste. Foy hospital services in Quebec. If I did not shy from it, I would recite a case which concerns me personally, since I am a pensioned veteran, and which would show how we are sometimes treated by the authorities of the Quebec Ste. Foy hospital.
90205-6-1184
Pension Act
I therefore ask the minister to inquire into the matter for the betterment of the hospital services provided in the Quebec area for our veterans.
Mr. Chairman, let me conclude by saying that 1,250,000 veterans will surely be happy to see our government enact this new legislation. For my part, I support this resolution.
I am sure that under the command-I can use that word-of the minister, our veterans will be proud of the present and will continue in the future to enjoy any new legislation he will introduce.
If we can express ourselves freely today and if we can look forward to the future with confidence, we owe that privilege to those who fought in the Canadian forces, to those disabled veterans who suffered the horrors of war, but who, thanks to their sacrifice did enable us to preserve the liberties which we so dearly cherish.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief in my remarks. May I begin by stating, as other members have stated, that the veterans of Canada will indeed be very proud of this legislation and happy to know that their situation and circumstances have been recognized by the government. I congratulate the minister on bringing in this legislation at this time and also on the assumption of the portfolio in which he now finds himself where I am sure he will be as successful as he was in his former portfolio.
In a previous session I brought to the attention of the house the fact that certain inequities exist in the administration of pensions, and that is my reason for speaking today. I did so on July 10, 1959, and therefore I wish to put before the committee a couple of points I have in my mind. In order that I may be clearly understood in the beginning and not called to order as I probably could be, may I say that I trust the minister-and I am sure he will in the not too distant future-introduce similar amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
It was indeed somewhat of a disappointment to me to hear the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont make a political argument by way of interjection in the debate, and under the circumstances I think he should have been called to order as another member was for being out of order in the remarks he was making. This is a

Pension Act
matter that concerns veterans and the Pension Act and certainly it has nothing to do with the subject matter that he was placing before the house. I might refer the hon. member to the discussion that took place in the house in 1946 when the minister and his parliamentary secretary were presenting legislation at that time comprising the veterans charter. On that occasion the minister particularly said that he appreciated the cooperation of the members of the Conservative opposition in making their views known in a non-partisan way. The interjection made by the hon. member this afternoon was anything but the type of co-operation that was sought at that time by his party when legislation and amendments were before the house.
The points I wish to bring to the attention of the house are simple and I will be very brief. The increase envisaged in the present amendment is certainly one that will be well received and I am sure it will raise the standard of living of those receiving medical pensions to a level which they justly deserve. In particular I hope that some consideration will be given in the legislation to the interpretation of the benefit of doubt clause, to which reference has already been made. I believe this matter was made very clear back in 1945. It has been pointed out to me on several occasions that the benefit of doubt clause was included for the clarification of particular cases in the minds of the pension commissioners. I do not believe that this is so. I think it was made very clear in the house on August 1, 1946 by Mr. Tucker, who was at that time the parliamentary assistant to the minister. He made these observations, as recorded at page 4179 of Hansard for that date, and I should like to repeat them now for the benefit of the committee:
Mr. Chairman, just to put it as briefly as possible, the Pension Act provides that if a disability is due to service it is pensionable; if it arises during service it is pensionable; if there is an aggravation of a condition which a man had when he went into the service, and he has had service in a theatre of actual war, and the disability was not obvious, wilfully concealed, or recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment, he not only gets pension for the disability in respect of the aggravation but he gets it in respect of the entire disability. Of course that does not apply in respect of service in Canada only. If he did not serve in a theatre of actual war he gets the pension in respect of the disability, or the aggravation of the disability, as the case may be, to the extent that there is an aggravation. That is putting it, I think, as simply as I can.
Now, in interpreting whether the disability arose during service or was due to service, we have the section which is in dispute today. The way it was worded before was:
"Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be

entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant."
That made the language as explicit, perhaps, as the English language could make it, that if there was any doubt whether this disability was incurred during service or was due to service, or the aggravation was incurred during service or was due to service, the applicant was to get the benefit of the doubt. I really do not see how it could have been made much plainer; but in deference to the committee and in accordance with what the hon. member for Vancouver South-
This indicates very clearly how the benefit of the doubt clause is to be interpreted. As a previous speaker mentioned, it may be time now to discuss again with the members of the pension commission their interpretation of the legislation that has been- brought down in the house.
I knew of one case in which a veteran was released from the service at the end of the first world war with a valvular heart condition. His own physician treated him for the entire period until he died in 1958 of a coronary. His widow did not receive any pension, so was advised to take the case before the appeal board. She did so and produced evidence from her husband's personal physician, but was again turned down by the appeal board. At this hearing before the board the man's personal physician stated, without any doubt, that the condition which the veteran had at the time of his discharge from the Canadian army resulted finally in his death. As a result of his ailment this man had been receiving a 49 per cent or 50 per cent pension, but on his death the board did not see fit to grant his widow any assistance. I feel this is an obvious case in which the benefit of the doubt clause was not used in its proper sense.
I feel, too, that it would be advantageous in considering the welfare of the dependents of pensioners in particular categories, possibly those with 50 per cent pensions or more, to study the possibility of granting the wife and the children under the age of 16 entitlement to hospitalization. If we are to accept the responsibility for the veteran in this particular category, and for his infirmities and disabilities, then I think we should be prepared to provide support in this way in so far as his dependents are concerned. I am sure some arrangement could be made by the Department of Veterans Affairs with the provincial governments to take care of the cost.
I should like to discuss other points that I had in mind, but most of them have been

discussed by other members. I shall, therefore, wait until the second reading of the bill to make any further remarks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first occasion on which I have had the opportunity, in my present capacity, of speaking on veterans affairs. I should like to say, first, what a pleasure it is to me to have been given the opportunity to serve this particular minister in this capacity. The record of the Minister of Veterans Affairs in service to his country, particularly in service to the military forces, is most outstanding as anyone can see by referring to his biography. He has had 26 years of service in the military forces and brings to his portfolio a thorough knowledge of veterans and their problems. He has a warm heart and a sympathetic understanding, which I believe are prerequisites of the minister of this department.
In so far as his predecessor Colonel Brooks is concerned, I should like to say how much all members of the house appreciated the efforts he made on behalf of the veterans. We wish him well in his career in the other place. May I say in regard to my own predecessor, who is now the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, that we extend our congratulations to him. I think I have the honour of being the first parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs who has a veteran for a wife.
The legislation which will follow this resolution, in addition to the increases in the pensions which have been referred to by the minister, will include provision for pensions on behalf of dependent children being continued until the end of the month in which the child reaches 16 or 17 and they will not stop on the day after the child's birthday, as is the case now. Then when the widow dies her pension and that of the children may continue to be paid to any person who is capable of assuming or has assumed the care of the children. Under the old legislation it could only be continued to a daughter. I am rather surprised that this amendment has not been introduced before now. I am glad to see it is being recommended to the committee.
If this legislation passes, additional pension may be paid to the woman who lives with a man for at least seven years and has been publicly represented as his wife. She may also receive the widow's pension upon his death, if she is otherwise qualified. This provision only applies in cases where the marriage cannot take place because of a previous undissolved marriage on the part of either party. I might point out that this provision has been contained in the War Veterans Allowance Act for some years.
Pension Act
Another of the resolutions which have been brought to the attention of the government by the Legion is that increases have been made in the last illness and burial expenses so that the maximum amount under this act may be available as under the veterans burial regulations.
I should like to say a few words about some of the resolutions which were drawn to the attention of the government by the Canadian Legion, particularly those that had been referred to hon. members in the course of the debate on this resolution. One of the resolutions put forward by the Canadian Legion is as follows:
Therefore be it resolved that we continue to press our demands that the government increase the rates payable under Schedules A and B of the Pension Act to bring them more in line with the wage index and standard of living.
I am extremely pleased, as I am sure are all hon. members, that it has been possible for the minister to give assent to that request. In dealing with the Legion resolution might I say at this time what a happy and fortuitous event it has been that the president of the Canadian Legion happens to come from my own constituency, namely Saskatoon. Professor Mervin Woods, who has had a distinguished career in law and in the teaching of law and long service in the armed forces and in the ranks of the Legion will bring to his task the wisdom, energy and ability which that great post demands.
If I may do so I should now like to say a few words with regard to the Legion resolution relating to special problems involving Newfoundland. Several of the Newfoundland members have spoken in support of the resolution put forward by the Canadian Legion to the effect that a change be made in the Pension Act in order to make clear the status of Newfoundland veterans in accordance with the spirit of negotiations leading up to the terms of union.
Every since the union of Newfoundland and Canada in 1949, under article 38 of the terms of union a Newfoundlander who served not in the armed forces of Canada but in those forces raised by Newfoundland and the United Kingdom has been required if he sought pension to apply first of all to the United Kingdom. Then, after having done that, he could apply to the Canadian pension commission for supplementation which would bring the total he received up to the Canadian pension standards, the same as any other Canadian. At this point I might perhaps just refer to the article in the terms of union to which I have made reference, namely term 38. It reads as follows:
38. Canada will make available to Newfoundland veterans the following benefits, on the same

Pension Act
basis as they are from time to time available to Canadian veterans, as if the Newfoundland veterans had served in His Majesty's Canadian forces, namely,-
I will skip paragraph (a) and go on to paragraph (b) which is the pertinent subparagraph, and which reads as follows:
(b) Canada will assume as from the date of union the Newfoundland pension liability in respect of the first world war, and in respect of the second world war Canada will assume as from the date of union the cost of supplementing disability and dependents' pension paid by the government of the United Kingdom or an allied country to Newfoundland veterans up to the level of the Canadian rates of pensions, and, in addition Canada will pay pensions arising from disabilities that are pensionable under Canadian law but not pensionable either under the laws of the United Kingdom or under the laws of an allied country;-
Hence the position of Newfoundland veterans was that if they were rejected for pensions by the United Kingdom they could still apply to the Canadian pension commission. This latter was a right which was not granted to Canadians who served in the allied forces up to the date of the introduction, and we hope eventual passage, of this particular resolution and bill. Up to the present time Canadians who served in the forces of the United Kingdom or in other allied forces could not apply to the Canadian pension commission unless the allied government granted them at least some pension. Once they obtained an award, they could apply to the Canadian pension commission to have that pension brought up to Canadian standards. However, if they were unable to qualify for a pension under the conditions laid down by the allied government those Canadians, unlike the Newfoundlanders, were precluded from applying to the Canadian pension commission for entitlement on Canadian grounds.
As was mentioned by the minister on December 12, as reported in Hansard on page 735, this form of discrimination will be removed by the proposed amendment. On that occasion the minister stated as follows:
Then with regard to Canadian citizens who served in allied forces during either of the wars, it is proposed to bring in an amendment so that they may claim entitlement from the Canadian pension commission when their claims have been rejected by the government of the allied force in which they served.
The Legion suggests in effect that article 38 of the terms of union be looked at in order to see whether Newfoundland veterans are entitled to go straight to the Canadian pension commission for a pension without reference to the United Kingdom at all and in effect to absolve the United Kingdom from any contribution at all to the pensions of Newfoundlanders who served in the United Kingdom forces-that is to say any

of the new pensions-or alternatively, although I do not think this was suggested by any of the hon. members who have spoken, that some sort of financial arrangement be worked out with the United Kingdom so that in the event that the Canadian pension commission awarded a pension in the first instance, to which normally the United Kingdom would have made a contribution, that contribution would still be made by the United Kingdom to the Canadian treasury in compensation.
The nub of the matter in so far as the Newfoundland veterans are concerned is simply this and no more than this. It is simply that they wish to avoid the time it takes in first making application to the government of the United Kingdom. I want to assure the Newfoundland veterans that their problems, just as are those of veterans in any other part of Canada, are of vital concern to me personally and to the Department of Veterans Affairs. I have had friendly relations with Newfoundlanders for many years. During the last war on many occasions I had the good fortune to stop in Newfoundland while going to and from Europe. I always looked forward to and enjoyed those stops and I have kept up some of the contacts I made on those occasions.
As a matter of fact, on first coming to the House of Commons in 1957 I had the pleasure of rooming with the hon. member for St. John's East and immediately struck up a lasting friendship with him which carried forward into work. He and I started a research project into the possibility of establishing transshipment ports in Newfoundland in order that grain could be kept stored in marketable position. The research that we started at that time is still going forward and as a matter of fact is broadening in order to provide marketable storage positions for grain in other places as well.
Therefore my relations with Newfoundlanders have always been warm and cordial, and may I say to the Newfoundland members that they may be assured that I intend to ask at the earliest possible opportunity for a study to be made of term 38 both by the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Justice, in order that the fullest consideration may be given to the representations which have been made both by the Canadian Legion and by hon. members of this house.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, in a very thoughtful address, mentioned the problem of conditions not recorded on enlistment. He referred to the Canadian Legion resolution on this matter, to the effect that section 13 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that where a pension applicant who served in an actual theatre of

war is found to have a disability resulting from an injury or disease not recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have occurred or have its inception subsequent to enlistment.
This particular point was referred to by other members in the course of their addresses. I think some question has been in the minds of the Canadian pension commissioners as to whether or not this particular proposal would in fact result in facilitating more generous awards. But I think this particular problem affords us a good opportunity for review in this house and in the veterans affairs committee and to bring this matter to the attention of the Canadian pension commission in order to have as full an explanation as possible of their attitude in regard to this matter.
Many hon. members spoke about the benefit of the doubt clause, and indeed the Canadian Legion had a resolution on that particular point also. Their resolution reads:
That the government take action to ensure that the benefit of the doubt as set forth in section 70 is in fact extended to all applicants under that act.
As hon. members know, the Canadian pension commission is an independent body and is in no way responsible to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, although it reports through him and although he is charged with the responsibility of bringing before cabinet recommendations for changes in any legislation affecting that commission. He is but the spokesman for the commission. The Canadian pension commission is responsible directly to parliament. Because of this it is very helpful to have the suggestions of hon. members expressed here and in the veterans affairs committee for the continued improvement in the way it functions.
Many members have made very useful and thoughtful suggestions in the course of this debate which I am sure will be of great help to the Canadian pension commission when it considers the report of this debate. Particularly, as I have mentioned, hon. members have made reference and many suggestions in regard to the operation of this benefit of the doubt clause.
One question I myself have heard on many occasions over the years, and upon which I would like to have some comment, is whether, in awarding pensions for nervous conditions or mental illness resulting from war service, sufficient weight is given by the pension commission to section 70 in dealing with these matters. Argument is made that mental conditions are with one from birth and if such conditions be considered for pensionable purposes at all they should be considered as to
Pension Act
the extent of aggravation of the nervous condition or mental illness due to war service. However, I would like to point out that my information is that this premise is not proved by any means. Much doubt exists as to the prime cause of mental illness, as well as some doubt as to the precise factors which increase its severity.
I would be very happy if the Canadian pension commission would reassess its stand in regard to this matter, giving full weight to sound, modern psychiatric knowledge and practices and to the benefit of the doubt clause. No veteran suffering from mental illness resulting from or aggravated by war service should be denied pension treatment unless there is no doubt that his illness did not in fact result from war service.
Another matter which might be considered in the committee is the resolution of the Canadian Legion to the effect that the additional allowances in respect of wife and dependents being paid to those pensioned at less than 50 per cent at the time of death be continued to the widow and such dependents so long as they remain eligible as otherwise provided under the act. Many members of the house have raised this question. It has been one of concern and one which I think would be capable of solution only by joining the experience of the members of the house and members of the committee with the experience of the Canadian pension commission.
The suggestion that allowances be continued to the widow and children after the death of the pensioner receiving less than 50 per cent pension is a new one in that particular term. It is of course closely akin to earlier suggestions that the widow and children receive pensions in cases where the pensioner is in receipt of less than 50 per cent disability pension and does not die of his pensionable disability. Might I suggest that this particular resolution receive, if it is considered appropriate by the veterans affairs committee, its attention for recommendation and suggestion.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury made a suggestion as to the composition of appeal boards. The Canadian Legion, too, had a resolution about this particular problem. The Canadian Legion urged the pension commission to ensure that all appeal boards are composed of one lawyer, one doctor and one layman, and if necessary reconstitute the board to make this possible. I understand that every attempt is made to follow the request contained in this particular resolution when appeal boards are being convened. The composition of appeal boards is, however, dependant upon a number of factors, including the composition of the commission

Pension Act
itself. Under existing circumstances I am advised that it is not possible to abide by the request contained in this resolution at all times, but that, as I point out, the commission does try to follow the request wherever possible.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo made some reference to earlier pension commissions. I gathered from the remarks the hon. member made that what he wanted was a brief review of the history of the various bodies which have been clothed with jurisdiction in pension matters during recent times. I have here a brief list indicating the various bodies which have had that jurisdiction from 1916 to date, and if it would be helpful to hon. members and the members of the veterans affairs committee I should like to place this list on the record at this time.
Order in council P.C. 1334 dated June 3, 1916 created the first organization to deal solely with war pensions. It was called the board of pension commissioners and consisted of a chairman and two members. It was expressly provided that there would be no appeals from decisions of the commission, but dissatisfied applicants could present their cases either personally or by counsel before the full commission sitting for the purpose of hearing the complaints of those who may have been dissatisfied with decisions given in the ordinary course of administration.
The next change occurred in 1919 by way of chapter 43, 9-10 George V. Statutory provision was made for a commission to be known as the board of pension commissioners, consisting again of a chairman and two members. I will not go into the duties of that commission other than to say that provision was made for two or more commissioners to sit for the purpose of hearing the appeals of dissatisfied applicants or pensioners. This provision was repealed when the federal appeal board was created in 1923.
In 1923, by way of chapter 62, 13-14 George V, the federal appeal board was created, consisting of a chairman and not less than four nor more than six members. This was abolished in 1930 by way of chapter 35, 20-21, George V. In that year a pension tribunal was created consisting of a chairman and eight members as well as a pension appeal court consisting of a president and two members.
In 1931, by way of chapter 44, 21-22 George V, the pension tribunal was increased to a maximum of 12 members with a minimum of 9 members, one of whom was to be chairman.
In 1933, by way of chapter 45, 23-24 George V, the board of pension commissioners and the pension tribunal were abolished and the Canadian pension commission was created consisting of a chairman and not less than

7 members nor more than 11 members. I believe this is the point about which the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo was inquiring. Provision was also made in 1933 for the hearing of dissatisfied applicants by quorums of the commission holding public hearings at convenient places throughout Canada. The pension appeal court continued as the final court of appeal.
In 1936, by way of chapter 44, 1 Edward VIII, provision was made for the appointment of ad hoc commissioners if and as required and not to exceed five. The procedure was amended to first hearing, second hearing, personal appearance and appeal. The quorums were continued and the pension appeal court remained as the final court of appeal.
In 1939, by way of chapter 32, 3 George VI, quorums were abolished and the pension appeal court was abolished and its power of final decision transferred to appeal boards of the commission to consist of three members of the commission holding sittings at convenient places throughout Canada. The procedure established consisted of first hearing, second hearing and appeal. Perhaps that summary may be of some use to hon. members in relation to this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will not long detain the hon. member for Lincoln, but I could not fail to rise after the parliamentary secretary spoke to express my disappointment at what he had to say about the Newfoundland veterans. As my friend the hon. member for Humber-St. George's indicated last night when I was unable to be in the chamber, I concur fully in. the representations made in their speeches by the other four hon. members on this side of the house from the province of Newfoundland. Our hopes were raised by the previous minister in 1957, the last time the act was opened. The then minister promised a study at that time and now the parliamentary secretary promises a study at this time of the same question. One wonders what has happened in the three-year interval.
Moreover, the parliamentary secretary did not say anything whatever about what, after all, is the largest single group of Newfoundland veterans who have what we think is a legitimate grievance. I refer to the forestry corps in Newfoundland. The mere fact that they were not enlisted men and did not wear a uniform in world war II, although they did

in world war I, has created the curious anomaly that although the Canadian forestry corps in both wars and the Newfoundland forestry corps in the first war are pensionable, the Newfoundland forestry corps in the second war are not, notwithstanding the fact that in the United Kingdom they worked side by side with the Canadians, did exactly the same kind of work and were subject to exactly the same sort of hazards.
It may well be asked what right have I to get up and say anything on this subject because from 1953 to 1957 I was a member of the government and was the representative in the government of the province of Newfoundland. While I admit all that, as my friend the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo pointed out, this problem was not brought to our attention at that time by these people. I am not saying it would necessarily have been dealt with if it had been but if we did not do what was right then that can be no excuse for not doing what is right now. I appeal to the government. Instead of giving the stock answer "Why didn't you do it?" the government should do it and get the credit that we might have got if we had done as we should have.

speechtext:
Honesty on the part of members of parliament does not surprise me. I think most hon. members on both sides of the house are honest. I was saying that this is an anomaly. It is something that is impossible to explain, except-as my friend the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo reminded me a moment ago before I rose to speak-by reason of the fact that the commission of government did not recognize these forestry veterans before confederation. It should also be remembered that the commission of government was not elected by the people of Newfoundland but was a government imposed on them. It was not a government representative of Newfoundland that failed to give this recognition.
I think it was unfortunate that it was not included in the terms of union. I am not saying there is any repudiation of the terms of union in not recognizing these forestry veterans. I am saying it is a matter of natural justice, of treating them on the same basis as they would have been if confederation had been in 1939 instead of 1949.
I am glad to see what the government is proposing to do for these older Canadians
Pension Act
who enlisted in the United Kingdom and allied forces in putting them on a level with the Newfoundlanders but one must remember that the Newfoundlander's position is quite different. The United Kingdom forces were the Newfoundlander's forces between 1939 and 1945. They were the only forces they could be expected to serve in, particularly in the air force and the navy. There was no Newfoundland navy or air force. A lot of Newfoundlanders had the good judgment to serve in the Canadian forces, but many of them did what was in Newfoundland the natural thing to do which was to enlist in the British forces.
And when they became Canadians on March 31, 1949 they were supposed to have all the rights of other Canadians presumably right back to the time of their birth because, in the Citizenship Act, they are described as being born in Canada. Therefore their position, it seems to me, should be assimilated in every way that it is legislatively and administratively possible to do it to the position that they would have had if they had been Canadians at the time they served in the forces. That is all we are suggesting, and I do hope that three years from now, or two years from now, we will not be told that still another study of this problem is going to be undertaken, because it really does not need any further study as the facts are all very simple, what it needs and all it needs is action.
Having said this, that is all I wish to say on this resolution. In fact, it strikes me that this resolution has been talked pretty threadbare already and I would suggest that if the Minister of Finance is as anxious to get on with his budget resolutions as he professed to be earlier today we stop this debate and get this resolution through and get back to the budget resolutions which we are ready to debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like other hon. members I do not wish to delay the passage of this resolution so that we might get along with the discussion of the bill and find out what the minister is going to bring forward in the way of amendments to the Canadian Pension Act. For these reasons, I will be rather brief. However, I would be remiss in my duty if I did not at this time on behalf of the many veterans organizations in my riding extend to the minister and all members of his department our most sincere thanks and appreciation for the consideration that they are giving to the many briefs that have been presented by the Canadian Legion and other organizations.

Pension Act
In my riding we have many veterans organizations. We have some eight branches of the Canadian Legion, including two Ukrainian and one Polish branch. We also have a branch of the Canadian corps and a branch of the good old British Imperial veterans. I am pleased that this year I will be able to become a member of the veterans affairs committee and I am looking forward to some very interesting sessions as a member of that committee. I might repeat what has often been said, namely that the Canadian Pension Act and the Canadian veterans charter are the most generous of any in the world today.
At this time, on behalf of the British Imperial veterans may I extend to the minister and his department their appreciation of the many benefits they receive from the Canadian government, which in many ways are equal to those of Canadian veterans. However, there is always room for adjustments and improvements and the draft resolution which the minister has submitted seems to open the door to many ways in which improvements can be made to the act. I will mention several of them which have come to me during my dealings with veterans in recent months.
There is the subject of section 36, subsection 3, of the Pension Act, which has been mentioned in this debate, and which I am sure has been reviewed on many occasions by the Department of Veterans Affairs. However, I do feel that it should be considered again. In its present form it does cause some hardship and sorrow when the veteran with a pension of less than 50 per cent dies and his pension stops; in other words, is not made available to his widow, which is the way the regulations read at the present time. I notice that this matter has been mentioned by other members and I trust the minister will give it serious consideration.
There is also the question of distribution of drugs and medicines to veterans receiving home treatment. In recent years it has become the practice in the department in some areas to have those drugs distributed through regional branches of the Department of Veterans Affairs. This often causes delay and in some instances the type of drug prescribed by the local physician is not always available at the veterans affairs branch dispensary. This is a matter which might be given some consideration.
Then there is the matter of borderline pension entitlement cases, especially those veterans who served long periods in the theatres of actual warfare. They should always get the benefit of the doubt. Even though there is too little evidence to substantiate a claim for pension it always brings much more satisfaction to a veteran who saw a lot of hard

warfare to get a pension for his disability rather than a veterans allowance.
I know that veterans allowances do not come under the Pension Act. Nevertheless, pensions for disabilities and for wounds and the veterans allowance for the burnt-out pensioner seem to go hand in hand. I trust that this part of the veterans charter will also be given consideration for amendment at this session of the house.
The matter of the British Imperial veterans who fought on the Afghanistan frontier in 1914 to 1919 and did not get victory medals and therefore are not entitled to veterans allowance might, I hope, be given further consideration by the veterans affairs committee during this session of the house.
I know that several other hon. members would like to follow me and I have quite a bit more that I should like to say. However, in order that they may be given an opportunity to voice their opinions at this time I am going to say that I appreciate the opportunity of speaking on behalf of all veterans and I am looking forward to learning more about the amendments to the Pension Act when the bill comes before the house.
