speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take great pleasure at this time in rising to make a few remarks in regard to the resolution to amend the war veterans' Pension Act. First of all I should like to associate myself with our many colleagues who have formally spoken on this amendment to congratulate the present Minister of Veterans Affairs. I am sure that if he carries on and creates the enviable reputation in his new portfolio that he did when he was the minister of trade and commerce he will make a very great contribution to this department.
I should also like to express my congratulations on behalf of my constituency and the great number of war veterans in it to the Hon. Alfred Brooks, the present minister's predecessor. I am sure they join with me in wishing him many happy years of contribution and benefits to the welfare of Canadians while he is in the other place.
I represent the constituency of Moose Mountain which has many active branches of the Canadian Legion. I feel it is my humble duty to support this very timely resolution before the house, even though it is widely recognized that the legislation on the statute books at the present time to assist war veterans, their widows and dependants, is the best in the world. Nevertheless, there is still room for certain improvements and these new proposals will certainly be appreciated by the million and a quarter war veterans in Canada today.

Pension Act
I suggest that since we are increasing the war veterans disability pension under the proposed legislation we should also, as soon as it is possible, endeavour to increase war veterans allowances by the same amount. Otherwise, as has already been pointed out by a large number of our veterans now receiving pensions, they would not benefit as they should under the proposed amendments to the legislation. I have had a number of representations from branches of the Canadian Legion in my riding emphasizing this point, and for the record I should like to quote one recently received from the Gainsborough branch No. 170. It is under date of January 23, 1961, and reads as follows:
Whereas the hon. Minister for Veterans Affairs has stated in the House of Commons it is the intention of government to make a substantial increase in the war veterans disability pensioners' pension at this session of parliament; and whereas any increase in the war pensioners' pension will not benefit to the extent of one cent any disability pensioner who is also in receipt of a war veterans allowance unless the war veterans allowance is also increased by the same amount as the war disability pensions;
Therefore be it resolved that the hon. Minister for Veterans Affairs be petitioned to ask parliament to increase the amount to war veterans allowance recipients as, if and when the promised substantial increase in war disability pensions is instituted and brought into force.
This resolution was moved by G. Meredith and seconded by J. W. Plumb and the communication is signed by their secretary, Mr. W. A. Slade. I cite this as an example of the representations made by a number of our Legion branches.
I should also like to say that like other hon. members I have had complaints from war veterans with respect to how the pension commission interprets what is commonly referred as the benefit of doubt clause. It would appear that at times the pension commission may be placing too much emphasis on or showing too much concern for treasury board rather than the needs of the war veteran applicant. I feel that the commission should try to get closer to the intent of the legislation than would appear to be the case in some instances now. In other words, the emphasis with regard to the benefit of the doubt clause should be transferred from the saving of money for treasury board to the needs of the war veteran applicant himself.
I could cover other suggestions that have been made by other hon. members but I feel that they made their points very effectively and that anything I might say would be superfluous. I should like to congratulate the new Minister of Veterans Affairs on introducing these amendments to the Pension Act. I am sure all Canadians will welcome this action of the government.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution has been anticipated by the veterans of Canada for some time. While increases in income have been granted to other groups in our economy, our veterans have been waiting patiently for their turn to come. It will be remembered that the former minister, the Hon. Alfred Brooks, hoped to have this legislation reviewed at the last session but it was found necessary to defer that review until now.
May I take this opportunity to join with other hon. members who have extended congratulations to the former minister, the Hon. Alfred Brooks on his elevation to a new sphere of responsibility and to wish him every success and happiness in his new work.
I would also join with other hon. members in their congratulations to the new Minister of Veterans Affairs on his appointment to this important portfolio and in their congratulations also to the new parliamentary secretary to the minister. We wish them both every success and satisfaction in their new undertakings.
There is no legislation processed by the parliament of Canada which is received with greater satisfaction than that which aims to improve the standard of living of those who served our nation in its time of need. Military service in the army, navy or air force involves the offering by those in the services of their time, their talents, their health and, if necessary, life itself.
Veterans legislation in Canada dates back for more than 40 years to the days of world war I and to the promise that was given by the government and the people of Canada that the economic status of the survivors of that conflict and their dependents would be protected. This undertaking was extended to the veterans of world war II and to those of the Korean conflict and the resulting legislation became known as the veterans charter.
The survivors of world war I are no longer young and many require more generous assistance than they are receiving. These increases in disability pensions can do much to add comfort and peace of mind to our older veterans' declining years. It is 20 years since the disasters of world war II threatened the loss of freedom to Canadians as well as to our allies in the struggle. Those were dark days when neither the enormity of the cost nor the enormity of the sacrifice was permitted to stand in the way of an all-out war effort. We found ways to finance our wars. We should be ready to fulfil the obligations growing out of those wars. Let time not dull the public memory of our great wars. Many suffered the loss of loved ones. Many were totally or partially disabled and many are reaping more and more as time goes on the

Pension Act
physical results of nervous tension and mental turmoil associated with war service. Our nation should not weaken in protecting the economic status of those whose sacrifice bought victory.
There are three particular matters in connection with this legislation which I should like to stress for consideration. I think all of them have been supported by other hon. members in this debate. I would suggest to the minister that consideration be given at this time to arranging for increases in veterans allowances. Many veterans in the lower percentage pension classes depend for their livelihood on a combination of a pension payment and a war veterans allowance payment. Since war veterans allowance payments are subject to a means test, increase in pension payments will result in decreases in their war veterans allowance payments. This is likely to cause hardship for some veterans, and I would urge the minister to take the necessary steps to avoid such a situation.
This will involve, I believe, changes in the war veterans allowance schedule and in the income ceilings under the War Veterans Allowance Act. I would urge that this matter be given immediate consideration to the end that increases in both disability pensions and war veterans allowances, which support each other, can be brought in simultaneously.
Another feature of the Pension Act which I find difficult to justify is that widows of pensioners who have been allotted a 50 per cent or higher disability are provided with widows' pensions whereas widows of pensioners who have been allotted a disability of less than 50 per cent are provided with no such pension. It is difficult to justify on moral grounds why this should be so and I urge upon the minister and the house that consideration should be given to amending subsection 3 of section 36 of the act so that all widows will be treated alike.
As the third feature which I wish to discuss I should like to add my support to those who have spoken in the debate and urged the full use of section 70 of the Pension Act which provides that in awarding pensions the board of pension commissioners shall allow the benefit of the doubt in favour of the applicant. I must say I would agree with the hon. member for Red Deer and others that an amendment to section 70 is unnecessary. What is required is a more generous interpretation of this section as far as the veterans are concerned.
I wish on behalf of the veterans, as well as of all citizens of Middlesex West, to express our appreciation to the minister and the government for bringing this legislation

before parliament. We believe it is necessary to assist in bringing our national obligations to our war veterans more nearly into line with modern costs of living.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all veterans in the house are very pleased indeed at the recent appointment of the new minister. Certainly, he is following a very able man. I would say that under Colonel Brooks we were, indeed, happy in the veterans committee and elsewhere, and I know that this situation will be continued under the present minister in the years to come. This was a good set-up because it must be a happy group that administers veterans affairs. The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador expressed the feeling of all hon. members when he said that inquiries which were directed to this department were handled with courtesy and promptness. This, in itself, is something which commends that department.
I should like to say a word about legions generally. I am proud to belong to the Legion. I am proud of the fact that we meet and that when we do, we remember. Those who attend these Legion meetings regularly must realize how wonderful it is that the veterans have banded themselves together. They perpetuate this wonderful spirit which has been developed by the veterans through two wars.
When the minister introduced the resolution he quoted some rather significant figures. He said that about $47.5 million have been added to the amount expended on veterans affairs. He referred to the changes in disability pensions, war veterans allowances, the increases in widows' and dependents' pensions, educational assistance and the increase in the cost of hospitalization. Apart from all these monetary increases, these various pieces of legislation which have come under review have been broadened extensively as to the classifications covered and the eligibility of the various classes.
May I also commend the parent branch of the Legion for the briefs that have been prepared. These have been of great assistance to all members of parliament, but particularly to those who have been members of the veterans committee and who have had the opportunity of welcoming the Legion representatives when these briefs were presented to the committee. All members of parliament have also received a large measure of aid from the Legion and from other veterans organizations. This help has been given voluntarily, whether it has been to-trace a person or for any other matter. It has been given, of course, with good heart.

I was particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer. He has a very broad knowledge of veterans affairs. Not only did he serve in two wars with distinction, but after these wars he turned to service in veterans affairs. During the course of that time he has dealt with many cases, and many veterans and their widows have come to him for advice. He summarized all the points very well. I am not overlooking the fact that many other members brought up points, too.
In so far as section 70 is concerned, it appears to me that the veterans committee must have a good look at it. We must ascertain whether it is necessary to have all these appeals, and why 50 per cent of them were granted. Anyone who has dealt with veterans or their widows must know that there is a period during which these people feel nothing is being done for them. They ask you right away, why cannot something be done about this? You say, there is a right of appeal, and it is this time lag that should be eliminated. The suggestions of the hon. member for Red Deer were excellent. He mentioned the need for a refresher course for pension advocates, and I believe that would be an excellent thing, to bring them up to date so that the handling of these cases will be more expeditious.
Surely, we must have reached the point now where a precedent has been set. If these precedents were followed, then the doctors and pension advocates would realize at once whether a case fell within the scope of these precedents and whether there was a chance the veteran would receive a pension.
I was rather surprised at the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, remarks which would indicate that those who were speaking on this resolution were holding up the business of the house. He inferred they should sit down and let the house get on with other business. He said he had followed the debate with interest, but rather left the impression when he sat down that nobody else should speak. The majority of the members who have spoken on this resolution have been veterans, and have been members of the veterans affairs committee. When we get up and say these things we say them not in order to prolong the debate but because we feel that a multiplicity of voices will bring these matters to the attention of those in authority. We make these representations in all sincerity and we will not be shushed by one member.
I was very pleased to hear the minister's parliamentary secretary make a reference to

Newfoundland during the course of his remarks. Certainly the members from Newfoundland, without exception, have put Newfoundland's case forward very well. Probably the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was the-

I am hoping that will be so. If there is a rejection, then he comes under our Canadian pension commission. Even if he is granted a pension over there he might not be eligible for a pension of the same extent as if he had been granted a pension by our own Canadian pension commission.
There are many other points I should like to cover, but they will be perhaps best covered after the bill has been introduced. I started out by saying that we are a happy group in veterans affairs. That is the situation. In my opinion the veterans and the Legion who follow these proceedings cannot help feeling that we are putting our best foot forward and are getting to grips with the many problems which are involved and the many anomalies which exist in the acts forming the veterans charter.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is my first opportunity to address myself to legislation under the new Minister of Veterans Affairs. He knows that I would be the first to acknowledge his gallantry in the last war and in the previous war and also to acknowledge with the same enthusiasm that he resembles his predecessor in qualities. I refer to the present Senator Brooks who had been in this Department of Veterans Affairs.
I think we have been fortunate in this particular department in that no veteran at any time, under one government or another, would have any feeling that he had not had

Pension Act
a man of spirit or gallantry at the head of this department. I think of Hon. Ian Mackenzie, Hon. Milton Gregg, V.C. and Hon. Hugues Lapointe. Steadily in this department, one government or another has placed in this office soldiers of great quality in whom the entire country would have confidence. I have confidence in the new minister. To him, valiant soldier that he has been, I know the veterans can look with great confidence in the future.
On the other hand, it is our duty to examine in parliament legislation as it comes before us. In this instance we are looking at legislation that involves a decision of members of a government with respect to pension entitlement. While I commend the resolution coming in at this time, it is only to be expected that I would say that in the opinion of the minister's predecessor this date is late. Being late it has proved to be extremely costly to those pensioners to whom so many tributes have been paid today and yesterday in this House of Commons debate.
Hon. Alfred Brooks, the predecessor of the present minister, had indicated that this kind of payment out to pensioners who need it would be given a year ago. He made that statement, but apparently his colleagues in the cabinet did not agree with him. The result is that a year or more later we have this type of legislation. This situation is evident as will be found if anybody will look at the printed record of the standing committee on veterans affairs meeting on April 7, 1960. At that time the then minister of veterans affairs was the first witness before the committee. As it happened, I personally chanced to be the one who asked him about the delay in doing something about which there had been a previous public commitment. I refer my colleagues now to page 131 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of that committee on April 7, 1960. I stated as follows:
Mr. Chairman, I would just refer to the editorial in the March issue of the Legionary.
That is March, 1960. That is the Legion's monthly publication.
At the committee sittings I said:
I think the Minister has it in his hand.
I just happened to notice that he had the red-coloured magazine in his hand. I continued:
The editorial, of course, quotes from the minister's statement in the House of Commons last year which read this way:-
I want to quote back what the minister said then, and I quote now to this committee as follows:
As I told the president of the Canadian Legion when he visited our office, it is not our intention to make any amendment this year-

That would be 1959.
-to the Pension Act. We plan to have it before us at the next session of parliament-
That would be the 1960 session of parliament.
-at which time we will go very thoroughly into all phases of the Pension Act.
Mr. Chairman, I just want to make everyone aware of facts, namely that the then minister of veterans affairs-I refer to Hon. Mr. Brooks-made this commitment in 1959 and I am sure that he made it in the utmost sincerity. However, I think that the present Minister of Veterans Affairs was at that time in the cabinet; and I think we are entitled to find out why, when a minister made that commitment in 1959 about something that was to be effective with respect to these deserving people throughout 1960, it did not become effective then. It only becomes effective in 1961.
In addition, I want to remind the committee that notice of this legislation came before us prior to the Christmas-New Year's adjournment. The committee on veterans affairs was set up prior to Christmas. I have been a member of that committee for a great number of years. As a member of that committee, at its initial meeting I raised the question, is there any chance that if we do not proceed to further meetings any veteran would be prejudiced by date of payment of any benefits under the new legislation?
In this resolution there is nothing to indicate whether a retroactive benefit is to be provided. However, I want to make it clear that in December, at its initial meeting, the veterans affairs committee indicated that it was willing to meet. As you know, Mr. Chairman, in normal circumstances members of the opposition do not want to have a committee meeting during hours when the House of Commons is sitting if that procedure can be avoided. However, at this meeting it was made clear that if any co-operation was required on the part of the opposition to meet when the House of Commons was sitting or otherwise we in the opposition were prepared to meet prior to Christmas if the government had no intention of putting in the bill a clause that would provide for retroactive payments to the veterans. On that day I asked the parliamentary secretary a question on this point and he said the contents of the bill could not be anticipated. But knowing the present minister and knowing his good will to veterans I am sure there will be no parliamentary prejudice.
Having read the speech from the throne, as all veterans have, I am sure the government will make it clear that any benefits shall have nothing to do with parliamentary

debate procedure, and will be retroactive in a way that will be of the utmost benefit to the veteran himself.
I say this after emphasizing that there was one complete year of delay, based apparently on the failure of the cabinet to adhere to a commitment made publicly by the former minister of veterans affairs in 1959. Otherwise all these needy people would have had in 1960 what is now afforded in the bill for 1961.
